newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's ruling Islamists on censure knife edge.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's ruling Islamists on censure knife edge.

text.p: Turkish Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan's hold on power was balanced on a knife edge ahead of a strong opposition bid on Tuesday to dump his coalition government for its Islamist leanings.
Deputies began debating a joint opposition bid to introduce a censure motion against the cabinet that will test Erbakan's wafer-thin majority.
"The government has put Turkey's long-term targets in danger," a parliament official said, reading out a joint motion from four opposition parties.
Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, earlier predicted he would survive what is in effect a confidence vote.

"Our government will see its vote of confidence renewed as the censure motion is thrown out once again," he told reporters. "So, God willing, this censure motion will give rise to a lovely day for us," he said.
Erbakan, who has a majority of only four MPs in the 550-seat assembly, has survived several previous censure motions, and an 11th-hour boost appeared to improve his chances.
Anatolian news agency quoted far-right leader Muhsin Yazicioglu as saying just minutes before the debate that he and his six MPs would back Erbakan.

The opposition motion requires a simple majority of those in parliament in order to go forward to a full debate on Thursday and a further vote on Saturday. But Turkish political tradition dictates a government resign if it loses the first round.
The government has been losing blood heavily since the secularist military began pushing it in February to stamp out rising Islamist activism.
A deputy from Welfare Party defected to the opposition on Monday in an unprecedented break in the Islamists' solidarity.
Three cabinet members from the conservative True Path Party wing have quit in the last month, citing unease at Erbakan's bid to increase the role of religion in public life.
One of the former ministers, Yalim Erez, has held extensive talks with the opposition to set up a secularist alliance against the Islamists.
But he has produced few details of much-vaunted plans for a shadow government of opposition MPs and True Path renegades.
The True Path leadership called its deputies into a closed-doors meeting on Tuesday in an attempt to ensure they all voted for the government.
"It has been decided to recommend taking a binding decision on the censure motion vote," parliamentary party spokesman Ahmet Uyanik told reporters.
Party leader Tansu Ciller, also the foreign minister, earlier held one-to-one meetings with backbenchers whose loyalty to the coalition is suspect.
Press reports spoke widely of huge "transfer fees" of up to $1 million being offered by both sides to win over fence-sitters.
The dispute between the Islamists and the powerful army has disrupted the government's plans to reverse a huge budget deficit with the help of $4.5 billion in privatisation revenues.
Istanbul's stock exchange, highly sensitive to political developments, firmed 0.8 percent in cautious trading ahead of the vote. The general index later rose slightly in early afternoon trading.
Brokers say the market is hopeful that secularists could form an "Islamist-free" government without going to elections if Erbakan were toppled.
